title: Joiner edits relationship details and gets an unexplained failure
preconditions: A created the space; B joined as the partner.
B opens Account and chooses Edit relationship.
B changes the anniversary date and saves.

actions.note: B opens Edit relationship and saves a new date.

expected_behavior: A non-creator is either not offered the edit action or told plainly that only the creator can change space details.
A failed save explains the rule and preserves the current values.
The UI never implies that the partner's change was saved.
candidate_failure_modes: The partner taps a working-looking Edit relationship row, fills the form, and receives only "Unable to save. Please try again."
The partner retries because the message implies a transient network problem.
The partner believes the anniversary date changed when the server rejected it.

observed_code_behavior: Spaces enforce one active membership per user and one active partner per space at the storage layer.
Joining redeems an invite once; an expired or already-redeemed code is rejected, and a historical partner slot is permanently bound.
Leaving flips the caller's membership to left and keeps shared history for the remaining member.
Space hydration, foreground refresh, and mutation callbacks are scoped to the signed-in user id.

hypothetical_user_behavior: A fictional participant (Vera Lind) said: "We are auditing Aoi for things that do not need to exist. Walk through the shared-memory flow you actually used this week: the composer, the Keep button, pending rows, retry and edit, author labels, the feed and gallery, empty and failed states, and every confirmation or helper line. For each one, ask out loud: "Why does this even exist?" Then say what would break if it were removed, and what it cost you. Name the three most useless things and the one thing you would keep. Do not propose a redesign; remove."

A fictional participant (Vera Lind) said: "I did the walk-through this week and I did it wrong on purpose, which is the only honest way to audit. Notes below. Not a redesign. A removal list.

THE THREE MOST USELESS THINGS

1. THE KEEP BUTTON. This is the one that made me say it out loud in a cafe. "Keep" is a verb with no object and no consequence. Keep what? Keep from whom? I pressed it, nothing was named, nothing was confirmed, and the row I "kept" looked identical to the row I abandoned. It exists to make me feel like I made a decision, which is exactly the fake-progress pattern I refuse to forgive. If it were removed, nothing breaks — the composer already holds the text and the row already exists. Cost: one guess, every single time, plus the low-grade suspicion that I have been silently discarding my own work.

2. THE PENDING ROW. A row that says "pending" and then... stays pending. Pending relative to what? Which clock? Pending is a status that refuses to name its own failure condition. When the action failed, the row did not change, did not say failed, did not offer retry — it just kept wearing the word "pending" like a polite lie. And here is the part I will not let go of: my input was still there, which means the app *had* my text and chose to hide the outcome from me. Ambiguous status with the data intact is worse than a plain error, because it proves the app knew and declined to say. If it were removed and replaced with nothing at all — just a row that either exists or is marked failed — the only thing that breaks is the illusion of background work.

3. THE HELPER LINE UNDER THE COMPOSER. It explains the thing I am already looking at, in a voice that changes depending on which state I am in, and it disappears the moment I actually need it — during failure. A helper that vanishes exactly when it would help is not a helper; it is decoration that costs me a re-read every time the copy shifts. Remove it. The label on the field was enough. It was always enough.

And the author labels. I am folding these into the above because they are the same sin at smaller scale: an avatar plus a name plus a handle plus a timestamp, on a screen where every post has exactly one author and I am not choosing between them. That is four signals doing one signal's job. One of them is lying about its precision, too — I cannot tell you what the timestamp is relative to.

THE ONE THING I WOULD KEEP

The failed state that preserves my input. I broke it deliberately — killed the connection mid-send, went back, hit retry, hit edit. My text was still in the composer, character for character, and edit put the cursor where I left it. That is the single behavior in this entire flow that respected me. It is also the reason the pending row is unforgivable: the app clearly knows how to hold my work and tell me the truth, and it chose to do only the first half. Keep that. Delete the rest of the ceremony around it.

Empty states: "Nothing here yet" with a full-width illustration is a modal that traps nothing and tells me nothing. If it were removed I would assume the same thing. Failed states: see above — the copy is inconsistent with the pending copy, two different vocabularies for the same event, which is the inconsistency I do not forgive. Gallery versus feed: two names for what is functionally one surface, and I had to guess which one held my kept item. I still do not know. I tried both. That is the whole problem in one sentence: I had to try both."
Vera Lind assumes: the app should never make me guess
Vera Lind assumes: a failed action must preserve my input
Wolf Adler assumes: a spinner is not a status
Wolf Adler assumes: a code field should accept a pasted message
